strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated weakness of CSCNNs (Zhdanov et al., 2024): the implicit kernel basis is incomplete for vector-vector interactions (missing frequency-2 components), demonstrated clearly for O(2,0) with analytical worked examples (Example 3.6, Appendix A.4-A.5).

The proposed fix is simple and well-integrated: conditioning the Clifford-steerable implicit kernel on an equivariant statistic of the input field (mean pooling) restores higher-frequency components at negligible computational cost (0.87% slower per Table 5).

The experimental evaluation is fairly thorough: four PDE benchmarks, 15 baselines with matched parameter counts, data-efficiency curves (Figure 2), a scaling study on SWE-5 (Table 2), a conditioning-operator ablation (Table 3), and an empirical equivariance check (Eq. 18) showing error of the same order as the unconditioned model (~3.4e-7).

The paper honestly labels the general completeness claim as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7), leaves its proof to future work, and includes a candid limitations section covering conditioning-operator simplicity, discretization-induced equivariance error, and inherited multivector-representation restrictions.
The improvement over the CSCNN baseline is consistent and substantial (e.g., -33.9% to -54.1% MSE per Figure 1c), and C-CSCNN is the best model on the fluid dynamics tasks (NS, SWE-1) in Table 1.
weaknesses: There is a logical gap in the central theoretical result. The proof of Proposition 4.5 (Appendix A.3) asserts that Eqs. 35-36 coincide 'if and only if' ρ(g)T[f] = T[ρ(g)f] (Eq. 38). This requires that the kernel network K̂ is injective in its conditioning argument, which is never established; a network can map distinct inputs to the same output, so the claimed iff does not follow. Since Lemma 4.2's steerability constraint must hold for all feature fields, this gap undermines the equivariance guarantee as stated and needs repair or a careful reformulation.

The headline theoretical contribution, completeness of the conditional kernel basis, is not actually proven. Section 4.4 only demonstrates that frequency-2 components become representable for O(2,0) (Example 4.6), yet the Limitations section claims 'we prove completeness for O(2,0)' — inconsistent with the body, which explicitly formulates Conjecture 4.7 and defers the proof. The central claim motivating the paper is therefore conjectural, supported only by empirics.

The contribution is incremental relative to prior work: conditional/input-dependent equivariant kernels are well studied (message passing, point convolutions, and non-linear equivariant maps per Nyholm et al., 2025, which the authors cite), and the conditioning operator actually used is plain masked mean pooling — a global mean-field that the paper itself concedes is 'less expressive'. The gap between the general framework (arbitrary conditioning) and what is validated (mean pooling) limits the significance of the empirical findings.

The method does not surpass the state of the art: Transolver outperforms C-CSCNN on both electrodynamics tasks (MW3, MW2) at every dataset size (Table 1), and on SWE-5 the 55M C-CSCNN trails CViT-S (13M) and CViT-B (30M) (Table 2), i.e., the equivariant model is less parameter-efficient than the attention baseline it is compared against. The SWE-5 comparison also mixes parameter counts inconsistently with the other tasks.

The incompleteness/incompleteness-fix analysis is carried out only for O(2,0), while experiments span O(2), O(3) and O(1,2); no comparable kernel-basis analysis is given for the other symmetry groups, so the mechanism behind the observed gains outside 2D Euclidean data is not established.

Presentation issues: proof-of-concept claims are supported by sympy printouts (Codes 1-3) rather than formal statements, Appendix A.3 contains a degenerate comparison (Eq. 37 equates identical left-hand sides), and there are multiple typos/grammatical errors (e.g., 'evaluation' → 'evalution', 'it is the part that is missing', 'os obtained', 'utilisationed') suggesting insufficient polish.
